title: Grid navigator
intro: A 2D array is an array of rows. `grid[r][c]` means row `r` first, then column `c`, both counted from 0.

rounds.right: Row first, then column: `{name}[r][c]` goes down to row `r`, then along to column `c`.

why.click: That's `{clicked}`: row {cr}, column {cc}. The first index picks the row (count down from 0), the second picks the column (count across from 0).
why.swap: That's `{clicked}`: row {cr}, column {cc}, so row and column are swapped. The first index is always the row.

rounds.right: `{name}.length` counts the rows and `{name}[0].length` the columns in row 0. Subtract 1 from either for its last index.

why.click: That's `{clicked}`: row {cr}, column {cc}. The first index picks the row, the second the column.
why.swap: That's `{clicked}`: row and column are swapped. The first index is always the row.
why.last: That's `{clicked}`. `{name}.length` is the number of rows and `{name}[0].length` the number of columns: subtract 1 from either to get the last index.
why.rows: `{name}` is an array of rows, so `{name}.length` counts the rows. Each row is a separate array, with its own `.length`.

rounds.right: Row by row, left to right: the nested loops read `{name}` like a page, and the {cells} letters spell {word}.

why.visited: `{clicked}` has had its turn already: the loops never go back.
why.skip: Not that one yet: `c++` moves one column at a time along row {r}.
why.column: The inner loop changes `c`, not `r`: it runs along the row first, and `r` only moves on when `c` reaches the end of the row.
why.jump: The outer loop hands out one row at a time, and the inner loop walks `c` along that row from 0. Which row is `r` on, and where is `c`?
